items.stem: A company virtualizes its entire datacentre and now runs several hundred VMs, but any new VM still requires a ticket a human approves within two working days. Business units are billed a flat internal rate regardless of how much they use. Is this cloud computing?

options.text: No. Without on-demand self-service and measured service, virtualizing the hardware alone does not satisfy NIST's definition.
options.why: Two of the five essential characteristics fail outright, and the definition requires all five, not the presence of virtual machines.

options.text: Yes — running many isolated VMs on shared physical hosts is the resource pooling NIST asks for, and pooling is the characteristic that decides the question.
options.why: Pooling VMs on shared hosts is virtualization, the enabling technology; NIST requires all five characteristics, and self-service and metering both fail here.

options.text: No, because NIST reserves the term for infrastructure a cloud provider owns, and hardware a company bought for itself can never qualify.
options.why: Ownership decides nothing here — a self-service, metered private cloud on owned hardware still qualifies; this environment fails on process, not ownership.

options.text: Yes — billing business units for what they use is measured service, and measured service is the characteristic the definition actually turns on.
options.why: Internal chargeback is not the same as usage-based metering, and neither substitutes for the self-service and elasticity NIST requires.

items.rationale: NIST SP 800-145 requires all five essential characteristics before an environment counts as cloud computing. Here, provisioning needs a two-day human approval (no on-demand self-service) and billing is a flat rate rather than metered usage (no measured service). Virtualization is the enabling technology beneath many clouds, but its presence alone — without the self-service, elastic, metered delivery model — does not make an environment a cloud.

verification.reasoning: Key checked against SP 800-145 s2: on-demand self-service requires provisioning 'as needed automatically without requiring human interaction with each service provider' (a two-day approval ticket fails), and measured service requires a metering capability (a flat internal rate is not metering). No distractor is defensible. Refuted on first pass because all three distractor texts had their own refutation appended after a semicolon, announcing which options were wrong; texts rewritten to state only the claim, with the refutation left in `why`.

items.stem: A team argues: 'This offering can't be cloud computing because there is no virtual machine involved — customers only invoke short-lived functions and are billed per invocation.' Is the team's reasoning correct?

options.text: No — NIST's definition does not require a VM; bare-metal instances, containers and functions are all valid cloud services as long as the five characteristics hold.
options.why: The absence of a customer-visible VM says nothing about self-service, elasticity or metering, which is what the definition actually turns on.

options.text: Yes — without virtualization creating an isolated VM per customer, there is no resource pooling and therefore no cloud, since pooling is the one characteristic that cannot be met any other way.
options.why: Resource pooling does not require a customer-facing VM; a provider can pool bare-metal or container capacity just as well.

options.text: Yes — function-based per-invocation billing is a serverless pricing pattern rather than cloud computing in NIST's sense.
options.why: Serverless and FaaS are themselves cloud service categories; billing per invocation is measured service in action, not evidence against being cloud.

options.text: No, but only because the provider also happens to offer a separate IaaS product alongside the function service.
options.why: Whether IaaS is also offered is irrelevant; the function service qualifies or fails on its own characteristics, not by association with another offering.

items.rationale: Cloud computing is a delivery model, not a technology, and nothing in NIST's definition names virtualization, containers or any particular vendor. Bare-metal instances, containers and functions are all cloud services in their own right provided the five characteristics — on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service — hold. Requiring a VM is exactly the false equivalence the guide warns against, just approached from the opposite direction.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 never mentions virtual machines; resource pooling is defined as the provider's resources being 'pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model', with no requirement of a customer-visible VM, and per-invocation billing is measured service. Key correct, distractors all false. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect in o3 and o4; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A hospital builds a private, self-service platform on its own hardware: clinical teams provision virtual capacity instantly through a portal, usage is metered per department, and capacity scales automatically with load. An auditor claims 'this can't be cloud computing — the hospital owns the hardware.' Evaluate the claim.

options.text: The claim is wrong — cloud computing is defined by the delivery model, not by who owns the underlying hardware, and this platform meets the essential characteristics.
options.why: NIST's characteristics say nothing about ownership; an organisation running its own private cloud is still cloud computing if self-service, elasticity and metering hold.

options.text: The claim is right, because true cloud computing requires a third-party provider operating shared, virtualized infrastructure.
options.why: Virtualization and third-party operation are common, not required; a private cloud on owned hardware satisfies the same definition.

options.text: The claim is right, because only public cloud infrastructure counts under NIST's model, and a platform confined to one hospital's own staff is not public by any reading.
options.why: NIST names private cloud as one of its own deployment models; it is not excluded from being cloud computing.

options.text: The claim is right, because on-premises hardware can never be billed by consumption — only depreciated as a capital asset over its service life.
options.why: Metering is a property of how usage is tracked and charged, not of where the hardware physically sits.

items.rationale: Cloud is a way of selling and consuming capacity, not a statement about who owns the building or the racks. A private cloud run by the organisation itself on its own hardware still satisfies NIST's definition provided the five essential characteristics — including self-service, elasticity and measured service — actually hold, exactly as this hospital's platform does.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 lists private cloud as one of four deployment models and states it 'may be owned, managed, and operated by the organization ... and it may exist on or off premises' — ownership does not disqualify. o3 is refuted by the deployment-model list itself. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect in o3 and o4; texts rewritten.

items.stem: Which five properties does NIST SP 800-145 require before an environment counts as cloud computing?

options.text: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service.
options.why: These are exactly the five characteristics NIST's definition lists.

options.text: On-demand self-service, broad network access, multi-tenancy, rapid elasticity, and pay-as-you-go billing.
options.why: Multi-tenancy and pay-as-you-go are real properties, but NIST folds them inside resource pooling and measured service rather than listing them as separate characteristics.

options.text: On-demand self-service, virtualization, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and high availability.
options.why: Virtualization and high availability are not among NIST's five; virtualization is an enabling technology and high availability is a design goal, not a defining characteristic.

options.text: Broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service, and vendor neutrality.
options.why: Vendor neutrality is not one of NIST's five characteristics at all, and this list also drops on-demand self-service entirely.

items.rationale: NIST SP 800-145 defines cloud computing through exactly five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. Plausible-sounding substitutes — multi-tenancy, pay-as-you-go, virtualization, high availability — are each real, but none of them is one of the five itself.

verification.reasoning: Key matches SP 800-145 s2 verbatim: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service. Multi-tenancy appears only inside resource pooling and pay-per-use only in the measured-service footnote, so o2's why is true. Refuted on first pass on two counts: the appended-`why` defect, and o4's option text referring to 'the exam's own scope' from inside the option; both fixed.

items.stem: An autoscaling group adds instances under load on Friday afternoon and removes them again over the weekend when traffic drops. Which essential characteristic does the weekend shrink specifically demonstrate?

options.text: Rapid elasticity, since capacity scales inward as well as outward to match demand.
options.why: NIST's definition explicitly includes scaling inward, and the weekend shrink is that inward direction in action.

options.text: Measured service — the bill only reflects instances actually running over the weekend.
options.why: That describes the billing consequence of running fewer instances, not the scaling behaviour itself, which is what the question asks about.

options.text: On-demand self-service — the system responds to demand without a human placing a request.
options.why: Autoscaling does act without human intervention, but the property being tested here is the inward-and-outward scaling itself, not who or what triggers it.

options.text: Resource pooling — many customers share the underlying hardware the instances run on.
options.why: Pooling explains why the capacity exists to be requested at all, but it does not describe the scaling behaviour the weekend shrink illustrates.

items.rationale: Rapid elasticity is often summarised as scaling up, but NIST's definition is symmetric: capacity must scale outward and inward to match demand. The autoscaling group growing on Friday and shrinking over the weekend is elasticity working in both directions, and the shrink is what lets measured service produce a smaller bill — a downstream effect, not the characteristic itself.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 defines rapid elasticity as capabilities 'elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand' — the inward direction is explicit, so the weekend shrink is elasticity. Each distractor names a real characteristic that the scenario does not specifically demonstrate, and each why is true. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage are vendor names for which underlying service category?

options.text: Object storage, the category behind buckets and HTTP-addressable blobs.
options.why: All three are the respective providers' object storage products, despite the different brand names.

options.text: Block storage, the category backing virtual machine boot disks.
options.why: The block-storage equivalents are Amazon EBS, Azure managed disks and Google Persistent Disk — a different product line entirely.

options.text: Managed relational database, the category behind SQL-compatible engines.
options.why: The managed database equivalents are Amazon RDS, Azure SQL Database and Cloud SQL, not these three products.

options.text: Identity and access management, the category behind users, roles and policies.
options.why: The identity equivalents are AWS IAM, Microsoft Entra ID and Google Cloud IAM, which none of the three named products provide.

items.rationale: The three hyperscalers sell a close to one-to-one mapping of service categories under different brand names. Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and Cloud Storage are each the provider's object storage product — recognising the category behind an unfamiliar vendor name is the reasonable expectation the exam sets, not memorising pricing or console navigation.

verification.reasoning: Key verified: the S3 user guide opens 'Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an object storage service', and Azure's storage introduction calls Blob Storage 'Microsoft's object storage solution for the cloud'. Refuted on first pass because the cited sources were the AWS and Azure availability-zone pages, neither of which mentions S3, Blob Storage, Cloud Storage or object storage at all — a wrong-source citation inherited from the concept's additional_sources. Retargeted to the S3 and Azure Storage overviews and the concept's sources widened to match; option texts also rebalanced so the one-word key no longer stood out.

items.stem: A question describes a fictional offering as 'a region-internal fault domain with its own independent power, cooling and networking' without naming a vendor. Which infrastructure unit is this describing?

options.text: An availability zone, which is AWS's and Azure's shared name for an isolated datacentre grouping within a region.
options.why: Both AWS and Azure use exactly this term for the concept described, and Google Cloud calls the equivalent a zone.

options.text: A region — the provider's overall geographic footprint, and the smallest unit with its own independent power and cooling.
options.why: A region is the broader geographic area; the description is of one isolated fault domain inside it, and independent power and cooling belong to that zone, not to the region.

options.text: A hyperscaler — one of the three major public cloud providers, each of which operates exactly one such fault domain per region.
options.why: Hyperscaler names the class of company, not a unit of datacentre infrastructure, and a region routinely contains several such zones.

options.text: A private cloud, since dedicated power, cooling and networking imply infrastructure reserved for a single customer.
options.why: Nothing in the description restricts use to one customer; isolation of power and networking is about fault domains, not exclusivity of tenancy.

items.rationale: The exam is vendor-neutral in its wording but expects the candidate to recognise the category or unit being described. 'A region-internal fault domain with independent power, cooling and networking' is precisely how availability zones are defined across providers, whatever brand name a specific question attaches to it.

verification.reasoning: Azure's availability-zones overview states each zone 'has independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure' and that zones are 'separated groups of datacenters within a region'; the EC2 page states 'Availability Zones are multiple, isolated locations within each Region'. Both cited sources genuinely carry the sentence. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten and o2/o3 whys extended to stay true of the new wording.

items.stem: Two teams each rent capacity from the same provider. Team A installs and patches its own guest operating system on a rented virtual machine. Team B pushes an application build and selects a supported runtime version, with the provider patching the OS beneath it. Which model is Team A using, and what is the deciding boundary against Team B's model?

options.text: Team A is using IaaS; the boundary is who owns the operating system, which IaaS leaves to the customer, while Team B's model puts it below the provider's line.
options.why: NIST gives the IaaS consumer 'control over operating systems' and denies the PaaS consumer control of 'the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems' — OS ownership is exactly that boundary.

options.text: Team A is using PaaS; the boundary is who chooses the runtime version, which is the one decision the provider never delegates.
options.why: This swaps the two models — installing and patching your own guest OS is IaaS, and runtime choice is a PaaS-level concern, not what separates A from B here.

options.text: Team A is using IaaS; the boundary is which team is billed per second rather than per month, since only IaaS meters at second granularity.
options.why: Billing granularity is an implementation detail of either model and is not the responsibility boundary the scenario is testing.

options.text: Team A is using IaaS; the boundary is that Team B's workload runs as a container, which is what makes an offering PaaS rather than IaaS.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario mentions containers, and PaaS is defined by the deployment relationship, not by any particular packaging technology.

items.rationale: IaaS gives the customer fundamental resources — compute, storage, network — and leaves the guest operating system, from the boot loader upward, entirely to them: the same patch cadence and the same responsibility as a physical server. PaaS moves that OS-and-runtime ownership beneath the provider's line, which is the single boundary the guide identifies as separating the two models.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145: IaaS consumers deploy 'arbitrary software, which can include operating systems' and have 'control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications'; PaaS consumers 'do not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems'. OS ownership is the stated boundary, so the key is right and o2 inverts it. o4's why is true (packaging is not what defines PaaS). Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect and a key `why` that cited the guide for a line NIST states itself; both fixed.

items.stem: A critical kernel security patch is released. On a rented IaaS virtual machine, whose job is it to apply it?

options.text: The customer's — the provider's responsibility under IaaS stops at the virtualization layer and host operating system.
options.why: NIST's IaaS definition gives the consumer control of the operating system, and patching it is part of that control.

options.text: The provider's — because they operate the underlying infrastructure, patching runs all the way up through the guest operating system.
options.why: AWS's shared responsibility model puts the host operating system and virtualization layer on the provider and the guest operating system, 'including updates and security patches', on the customer.

options.text: Whichever party originally enabled automatic OS updates on the instance — enabling them transfers patching duty to the provider.
options.why: Enabling auto-updates is a customer configuration choice made within their own responsibility, not a transfer of that responsibility to the provider.

options.text: Neither — under IaaS the runtime is patched automatically by the platform, so no kernel patching is needed.
options.why: Automatic runtime patching describes PaaS; an IaaS instance is a raw building block with no such platform-managed runtime layer.

items.rationale: Renting a virtual machine does not rent an administered one. From the guest OS boot loader upward the machine behaves exactly like a server in a rack, so kernel patching, host firewall rules and application configuration remain the customer's work — the misconception that the provider covers this is the source of most wrong answers on shared responsibility questions.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 gives the IaaS consumer 'control over operating systems', so kernel patching is the customer's. The key's exact wording — the provider stopping at 'the virtualization layer and host operating system' — is AWS shared-responsibility-model language, and that page was not cited; refuted on that citation gap and on the appended-`why` defect. Fixed by adding aws-shared-responsibility-model (it states the customer 'assumes responsibility and management of the guest operating system (including updates and security patches)') and rewriting o2's why to quote it rather than the guide.

items.stem: A team provisions a virtual network and a set of block storage volumes from a provider, without touching any compute instance yet. Is this still an IaaS activity?

options.text: Yes — IaaS covers fundamental computing resources broadly, including virtual networks and storage volumes, not only virtual machines.
options.why: NIST's definition names processing, storage and networks together as IaaS resources; a VM is the canonical example, not the only one.

options.text: No — without a running virtual machine there is no IaaS resource in use yet, since the virtual machine is the only genuine IaaS product.
options.why: A virtual machine is the most familiar IaaS product, but the guide is explicit that provisioning a virtual network is still an IaaS question, not a non-answer.

options.text: No — provisioning storage and networking without deploying application code is a PaaS-level activity.
options.why: PaaS is defined by deploying application code onto a managed platform; raw storage and network provisioning with no application involved is squarely IaaS.

options.text: Yes, but only if the team also attaches a managed database to the network, since IaaS requires at least one managed component.
options.why: Attaching a managed database would make that specific component a managed service, but it has no bearing on whether the storage and network provisioning itself counts as IaaS.

items.rationale: A virtual machine is the canonical IaaS product, but IaaS also covers block storage volumes and virtual networks provisioned as raw building blocks the customer assembles themselves. A question about provisioning a virtual network, with no VM yet involved, is still an IaaS question for exactly that reason.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145's IaaS definition is 'to provision processing, storage, networks, and other fundamental computing resources' — networks and storage are named alongside compute, so a virtual network and block volumes are IaaS without any instance. o3 and o4 are false and their whys true. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: Three teams describe their setup: Team X writes application code and pushes it to a platform that runs the OS and language runtime beneath it. Team Y only signs in, configures settings and uploads data into a finished application they did not write. Team Z registers individual functions that start on an event and shut down when idle. Which team is using PaaS, and what single fact distinguishes it from the other two?

options.text: Team X, since PaaS is distinguished by deploying application code the consumer wrote, unlike Team Y's finished application or Team Z's per-event functions.
options.why: Who wrote the running code, and whether it is deployed as a whole application versus invoked per event, is exactly the axis separating the three models.

options.text: Team Y — PaaS is distinguished by needing no deployment artifact at all, only configuration of an application the provider already runs.
options.why: Needing no deployment artifact describes SaaS, Team Y's model; PaaS requires exactly the artifact Team X pushes.

options.text: Team Z — PaaS is distinguished by billing only for the duration code actually runs, so an idle platform costs nothing.
options.why: Pay-only-while-running billing is the FaaS property Team Z exhibits; PaaS typically bills for provisioned instances that stay warm even when idle.

options.text: Team X — PaaS is distinguished by the team never having to select a runtime version, because the provider pins it for them.
options.why: PaaS still requires selecting a supported runtime from what the provider offers; the provider patches it, but the choice remains the consumer's, much as IaaS leaves the whole OS choice to the consumer.

items.rationale: The three service models differ in what the consumer supplies and who wrote the running code. PaaS runs an application the consumer wrote on infrastructure the provider manages beneath the runtime; SaaS needs no deployment artifact because the provider's own application is what runs; FaaS invokes individual functions per event and, unlike PaaS, typically charges nothing while idle. Team X's arrangement — push code, provider runs OS and runtime — is PaaS on that basis.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 PaaS: 'deploy onto the cloud infrastructure consumer-created or acquired applications created using programming languages, libraries, services, and tools supported by the provider' — which makes the key right and o4 false (a supported runtime is still chosen by the consumer). SaaS is 'to use the provider's applications', refuting o2. o3's why relies on FaaS billing, which CNCF's FaaS entry supplies ('eliminating costs when functions are dormant, distinguishing it from ... PaaS, which require continuous resource availability') but which was not cited; refuted on that gap plus the appended-`why` defect, and fixed by adding cncf-glossary-faas.

items.stem: A platform team pushes their application weekly but discovers the bill is unchanged whether traffic is high or completely absent overnight. Why does PaaS behave this way?

options.text: Most PaaS platforms bill for provisioned instances that stay warm, so an idle application still costs money even with no traffic.
options.why: CNCF's FaaS entry draws exactly this line: FaaS eliminates costs when functions are dormant, 'distinguishing it from other models like Platform as a Service (PaaS), which require continuous resource availability'.

options.text: PaaS scales to zero automatically whenever traffic stops — so a flat overnight bill can only be a billing error worth disputing.
options.why: Scaling to zero and charging nothing when idle is the FaaS property, not PaaS's; a flat overnight charge for a PaaS app is expected behaviour, not a mistake.

options.text: PaaS charges a fixed subscription regardless of infrastructure used, the same as SaaS.
options.why: PaaS billing tracks provisioned compute resources, not a per-seat subscription; that billing shape belongs to SaaS instead.

options.text: PaaS means the team no longer needs to think about scaling at all, so cost is naturally constant.
options.why: Not having to manage servers is only half true — the team still configures scaling policies, and provisioned instances that stay warm are exactly why an idle app still costs money.

items.rationale: PaaS platforms usually keep application instances provisioned and warm so requests can be served immediately, and that warm capacity is billed whether or not it is handling traffic. That is precisely the line CNCF draws between PaaS and FaaS: FaaS scales to zero and charges nothing when idle, while PaaS's operational relief does not extend to its billing model.

verification.reasoning: The key is a billing claim SP 800-145 says nothing about; refuted on citation until sourced. CNCF's FaaS entry states FaaS eliminates cost while dormant, 'distinguishing it from other models like Platform as a Service (PaaS), which require continuous resource availability' — that is the key, and it also settles o2 and o3. Fixed by adding cncf-glossary-faas and regrounding the key's why on it rather than on the guide; appended-`why` defect also fixed.

items.stem: A team connects their application to a provider-operated managed database, but writes and deploys no application code onto the database itself. Does connecting to it make the database part of the team's PaaS usage?

options.text: No. Nothing of the team's is deployed onto the database, so it is a managed service rather than PaaS, even though the team's application is PaaS.
options.why: PaaS is defined by deploying consumer-created application code; a managed database the team merely connects to has no such deployment, which is exactly the managed-services distinction.

options.text: Yes — any provider-operated component that a PaaS application depends on is itself part of the PaaS model the application runs on.
options.why: Dependency is not deployment; the guide is explicit that a managed database you connect to is a managed service precisely because you never deploy an application onto it.

options.text: Yes, because the database runs on the same underlying infrastructure as the application, which is what puts it inside the same service model.
options.why: Shared underlying infrastructure does not determine the service model; what matters is whether the consumer deploys application code onto the component.

options.text: No, because managed databases are always billed on a separate invoice from application hosting.
options.why: Billing separation is not the deciding factor and is not even reliably true across providers; the deciding factor is whether an application artifact is deployed onto the component.

items.rationale: PaaS and a managed service both take work off the customer's plate, but the line between them is whose code is running: PaaS runs an application the consumer wrote, while a managed service runs a standard component the provider maintains. A team connecting to — rather than deploying onto — a managed database is using a managed service alongside their PaaS application, not extending PaaS to cover the database.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 defines PaaS by what the consumer deploys — 'consumer-created or acquired applications' — so a database the team only connects to falls outside it. o2, o3 and o4 are each false and their whys true; o4's why correctly notes billing separation is not reliably true across providers. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A company subscribes to a SaaS product, signs in, and an employee later shares a report link publicly by mistake, exposing customer data. Who is responsible for the misconfiguration?

options.text: The customer — sharing settings, access rights and what users upload remain the customer's responsibility even though the provider runs and patches the application.
options.why: SaaS shrinks the operational surface to almost nothing, but identity, access configuration and data sharing are exactly the residual responsibilities that survive at every service model.

options.text: The provider — SaaS means the provider is responsible for security end to end, including how customers choose to share the data they upload, which is why the incident is the vendor's to answer for.
options.why: This is the precise misconception the shared responsibility model exists to correct: the provider secures the application, but a misconfigured sharing link is the customer's failure regardless of service model.

options.text: The provider — since SaaS, unlike PaaS, gives the customer no configuration surface to misuse in the first place.
options.why: SaaS does expose limited user-specific configuration, including sharing controls, and misusing that surface is what caused the exposure here.

options.text: Neither — public exposure of a shared link is covered by the provider's published SLA, which indemnifies both parties.
options.why: An SLA addresses the provider's own availability commitments and remedies; it says nothing about a customer's data-sharing mistake.

items.rationale: SaaS is where the operational surface is smallest and the residual customer responsibility is most often forgotten. The provider runs and patches everything, but identity, access rights, data classification and sharing settings remain entirely the customer's — and a leaked report link is exactly that kind of failure, at any service model.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145's SaaS definition preserves 'limited user-specific application configuration settings' for the consumer, which is precisely the sharing surface misused here and refutes o3. The key's responsibility claim, however, is shared-responsibility-model content that SP 800-145 does not carry; refuted on that citation gap and on the appended-`why` defect. Fixed by adding aws-shared-responsibility-model, which states customer responsibility is 'Security in the Cloud' and varies with the service selected.

items.stem: A vendor bills a company per named user seat each month, regardless of how many of those seats actually log in. Is this billing pattern typical of SaaS, and why does it differ from IaaS billing?

options.text: Yes — SaaS is normally billed per-seat or per-tenant, so an unused seat still costs money, unlike IaaS and FaaS's usage-based billing.
options.why: NIST names 'active user accounts' among the units a cloud may meter, while CNCF sets FaaS's usage billing against it by 'eliminating costs when functions are dormant' — a seat charges for access granted, not usage taken.

options.text: No — SaaS should scale its billing to zero cost when a seat goes unused, exactly as PaaS does when an application sits idle overnight.
options.why: Scaling billing to zero on idle is not a PaaS property either — most PaaS still bills for provisioned instances — and it is even less true of SaaS's per-seat subscription model.

options.text: No — SaaS is metered per API call, the same usage-based billing IaaS uses, so unused seats cost nothing.
options.why: Per-call metering describes usage-based IaaS-style billing; SaaS's typical model is a flat subscription regardless of use.

options.text: Yes, and IaaS bills the same way, per named account rather than per resource consumed.
options.why: IaaS bills for the compute, storage and network resources actually provisioned and consumed, not for named user accounts.

items.rationale: A SaaS subscription is normally a per-seat or per-tenant fee charged regardless of use, which is why an unused licence still costs money. That is a deliberate contrast with IaaS and FaaS, both of which are billed on actual consumption — the difference is a service-model property, not an accident of one vendor's pricing.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145's measured-service clause names 'active user accounts' as one of the units a cloud may meter, which legitimises per-seat charging, and CNCF's FaaS entry supplies the contrast the key draws ('true pay-as-you-go ... eliminating costs when functions are dormant'). Refuted on first pass because the billing contrast was sourced only to SP 800-145, which carries no PaaS or FaaS billing statement, and for the appended-`why` defect; fixed by adding cncf-glossary-faas and regrounding the key's why.

items.stem: A managed message queue charges per message processed and requires no server administration from the customer, but no individual customer-written function is triggered per message — the queue itself is the product. Is this FaaS?

options.text: No — it is serverless without being FaaS; CNCF treats serverless as the broader term spanning PaaS-like through SaaS-like services, with FaaS the narrower, function-specific member.
options.why: FaaS specifically means individual event-triggered functions the consumer writes; a managed queue with no customer function is serverless in its operational model but not FaaS.

options.text: Yes — anything billed per use with no server management is FaaS by definition, since FaaS is simply the billing model's proper name.
options.why: Pay-per-use with no server management describes serverless generally; FaaS additionally requires that the unit executing is a customer-written, event-triggered function, which this queue lacks.

options.text: Yes — any component that avoids the continuous resource billing PaaS requires must be FaaS, because that gap is what the term was coined to name, whatever unit of work actually executes.
options.why: The billing pattern is a genuine FaaS discriminator against PaaS, but it does not by itself make every such component FaaS — this queue has no customer function at all.

options.text: No — it is a managed service, and managed services and serverless are mutually exclusive categories in CNCF's glossary.
options.why: They are not mutually exclusive; a serverless offering is very often also a managed service, since the provider operates it end to end.

items.rationale: CNCF calls serverless a comprehensive term spanning PaaS-like through SaaS-like services, with FaaS one specific member of it — a managed queue billed per message is serverless without being FaaS, because there is no customer-written, event-triggered function doing the work.

verification.reasoning: Both cited CNCF pages were fetched and do contain what they are cited for: the serverless entry says 'Serverless is a comprehensive term encompassing services with these attributes, extending from Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) to Software-as-a-Service (SaaS)', and the FaaS entry defines FaaS as 'executing event-triggered functions' and 'the deployment of individual functions'. Neither page says serverless and managed services are exclusive, so o4 is false. Refuted on first pass only for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A batch job runs continuously at high load for six hours a day, every day. A team considers moving it from a fixed-size PaaS instance to FaaS to save money. What is the risk in that plan?

options.text: Under sustained high load, FaaS's per-invocation pricing can cost more than a continuously running instance sized for the same throughput.
options.why: CNCF ties FaaS's economics to charging 'solely for the duration of computation', with no cost while inactive — a job at high load six hours a day is exactly where that advantage stops applying.

options.text: There is no risk, since serverless always eliminates cost when a workload is idle, and every workload is idle most of the day, batch jobs included.
options.why: This job is not idle — it runs at high load for six hours daily — so the idle-cost advantage that makes FaaS attractive elsewhere does not apply here.

options.text: There is no risk, since FaaS and PaaS bill identically for continuous workloads of the same throughput.
options.why: They do not bill identically — PaaS charges for provisioned capacity regardless of load pattern, while FaaS charges per invocation, and those can diverge sharply under sustained load.

options.text: The risk is that FaaS cannot hold state between invocations, which this batch job requires in order to run at all.
options.why: Statelessness is a real FaaS constraint, but the scenario describes a cost concern under sustained load, not a state-management requirement.

items.rationale: FaaS's economics come from charging only for computation and nothing while idle. A workload that is busy for six hours every day is far from idle, so the cost advantage that makes FaaS attractive largely disappears, and a continuously running instance sized for that throughput can end up cheaper — the guide's warning against assuming serverless is always the lower-cost choice.

verification.reasoning: CNCF's FaaS entry states 'Charges apply solely for the duration of computation, ensuring no costs accrue when functions are inactive' and contrasts this with PaaS, 'which require continuous resource availability' — which grounds the key's hedged claim that per-invocation pricing *can* cost more under sustained load, and refutes o3 outright. o4's why correctly concedes statelessness is a real FaaS constraint ('emphasizing its stateless nature') while noting it is not the risk asked about. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect and a key `why` grounded on the guide rather than CNCF; both fixed.

items.stem: A regulator asks whether customer workloads on a public cloud platform are visible to other tenants, since the service is 'open to the public.' What is the accurate answer?

options.text: No — 'public' describes who may buy the service, not who may see a customer's data; tenants are logically isolated by separate accounts, networks and encryption keys.
options.why: NIST defines public cloud by who may use the service — 'provisioned for open use by the general public' — while SP 800-146 describes tenants' workloads as 'separated only by access policies implemented by a provider's software', which is isolation, not visibility.

options.text: Yes — anyone who can purchase the service can also see any tenant's data stored on it, since the storage layer is genuinely shared.
options.why: This is the misreading the term invites; isolation is enforced by the virtualization and identity layers even though the physical estate is shared.

options.text: No, but only because this workload must actually be running in a private cloud rather than a public one, which by itself would rule the platform out of the public category.
options.why: Nothing about the scenario suggests the workload has moved to a private cloud; public cloud tenants are isolated from each other by design, which is sufficient on its own.

options.text: No, because public cloud providers only sell to businesses and governments, never individuals — the tenant set is vetted in advance.
options.why: NIST's definition allows open use by the general public and says nothing about restricting buyers to organisations; isolation, not the buyer's identity, is what protects the data.

items.rationale: NIST defines public cloud as infrastructure provisioned for open use by the general public — a statement about who may purchase the service. Customers are separated logically through accounts, virtual networks and encryption keys while sharing the same physical estate, so 'public' never implies that one customer's workload is visible to another.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 says only that a public cloud is 'provisioned for open use by the general public' — a statement about availability, which refutes o4 — but says nothing about tenant isolation, so the key's isolation claim was unsourced; refuted on that gap plus the appended-`why` defect. Fixed by adding SP 800-146, which states 'The workloads of different clients may reside concurrently on the same system and local network, separated only by access policies implemented by a provider's software'.

items.stem: A finance director assumes moving a steady, predictable, high-volume workload to public cloud will automatically cut costs. Is that assumption safe?

options.text: No — public cloud's advantage is elasticity and speed, and steady, predictable, high-volume workloads can be cheaper on owned hardware.
options.why: SP 800-146 puts the benefit in elasticity — avoiding 'excessive costs from over-provisioning' — and adds that whether cloud reduces overall costs 'depends on a careful analysis of all the costs'.

options.text: Yes — public cloud infrastructure is always cheaper than owning equivalent hardware, because providers buy at a scale no single customer can match.
options.why: This treats elasticity's benefit as universal; a workload that never varies gains nothing from elastic capacity it never needs to use.

options.text: No — steady workloads should run on private cloud instead, since private cloud is always the cheaper deployment model.
options.why: Private cloud is not inherently cheaper either — its usual motivations are regulation, residency and control, not cost — so this does not follow from the scenario.

options.text: Yes, because public cloud eliminates capital expenditure for any workload shape, and operating expense is always the cheaper of the two.
options.why: Avoiding capital expenditure is real, but it is only one factor; a steady high-volume workload may still cost more over time on a public platform than on owned hardware sized for it.

items.rationale: Public cloud's selling point is elastic capacity and speed of provisioning, not an automatic price advantage. A workload whose demand never varies gets no benefit from elasticity and can be cheaper to run on owned hardware sized precisely for it — assuming the move always saves money is the trap the guide calls out directly.

verification.reasoning: The key is an economics claim that SP 800-145 does not address at all — refuted on citation on the first pass. SP 800-146's executive summary settles it: elasticity lets customers 'avoid excessive costs from over-provisioning, i.e., building enough capacity for peak demand and then not using the capacity in non-peak periods', and 'Whether or not cloud computing reduces overall costs for an organization depends on a careful analysis of all the costs of operation, compliance, and security'. Added as a source; o3's why (private cloud is not inherently cheaper) is true and no distractor is defensible. Appended-`why` defect also fixed.

items.stem: A third-party provider owns, operates and hosts an off-premises platform dedicated to exactly one client organisation, with self-service provisioning and metered chargeback to that client's business units. Which NIST deployment model is this, and why does location not decide the answer?

options.text: Private cloud — NIST defines it by exclusive use by one organisation, and explicitly allows the infrastructure to be owned, managed and operated by a third party, on or off premises.
options.why: Exclusivity of use, not physical location or ownership, is the criterion NIST states, and this scenario satisfies it exactly.

options.text: Public cloud — since a third party owns and operates the infrastructure rather than the client itself, and third-party operation is what the public model names, on or off the customer's premises.
options.why: Third-party operation is common to both models; what makes this public or private is who may use it, and here use is restricted to one organisation, which is private cloud.

options.text: Not a cloud at all, since the client organisation does not own the hardware it provisions capacity on.
options.why: Ownership is irrelevant to whether this is a cloud; the self-service provisioning and metered chargeback described are exactly the essential characteristics that make it one.

options.text: Hybrid cloud, because the infrastructure is hosted off the client's own premises while the client's users remain on them.
options.why: Hybrid requires two or more distinct cloud infrastructures bound together with portability between them; a single dedicated platform, however it is hosted, is not that.

items.rationale: NIST's private cloud definition turns on exclusivity of use by a single organisation, and it explicitly permits that infrastructure to be owned, managed and operated by a third party, on or off premises. An off-premises, third-party-operated platform dedicated to one client is exactly the case the definition anticipates — the common assumption that private cloud must be on-premises and self-run is the trap.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 verbatim: private cloud is 'provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization', and 'It may be owned, managed, and operated by the organization, a third party, or some combination of them, and it may exist on or off premises' — the key restates the definition and o2 and o4 are refuted by it directly. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A company runs a virtualized server cluster entirely inside its own building, with no self-service provisioning, no elastic scaling and no usage metering — capacity requests go through a manual ticket. Is this a private cloud?

options.text: No — without on-demand self-service, elasticity and metering, it is a virtualized datacentre rather than a cloud of any deployment model, private included.
options.why: Private cloud is still cloud computing first; the essential characteristics must hold before the private-versus-public distinction is even relevant.

options.text: Yes — any on-premises infrastructure dedicated to one organisation counts as private cloud regardless of how it is provisioned or how long a request takes to fulfil.
options.why: On-premises and dedicated to one organisation are necessary but not sufficient; the environment must also meet the essential characteristics, which this one plainly does not.

options.text: Yes, since it is not open to the general public and therefore falls under the private cloud model by elimination.
options.why: Not being open to the public rules out only public cloud, not the possibility that this is not a cloud at all — process failures on self-service and elasticity are the actual disqualifier.

options.text: No, because private cloud requires third-party hosting, which this arrangement lacks entirely, leaving it outside every NIST model.
options.why: NIST allows the organisation itself to own, manage and operate a private cloud; third-party hosting is not required, so this is not the disqualifying factor here.

items.rationale: A private cloud is still, first and foremost, a cloud: the five essential characteristics must hold before the question of which deployment model applies even arises. A virtualized cluster with a manual ticket process, no elasticity and no metering fails that first test entirely, so it is not a private cloud — it is simply a virtualized datacentre.

verification.reasoning: A private cloud is still a cloud: SP 800-145 states 'This cloud model is composed of five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models', so the characteristics must hold before a deployment model applies. A manual ticket process fails on-demand self-service ('without requiring human interaction with each service provider'), and there is no metering. o4's why is true — NIST allows the organisation itself to own, manage and operate a private cloud. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A provider offers a single-tenant dedicated host inside its otherwise open public cloud platform, reachable through the same self-service console as every other customer's shared instances. Is the dedicated host best classified as a private cloud?

options.text: No — the surrounding cloud infrastructure is still provisioned for open use by the general public, so a single-tenant host within it reads better as a public-cloud feature than as its own private cloud.
options.why: The guide treats this exact case as an application of the definition rather than a literal quotation from it, and the reasoning is that the platform around the host remains open to any customer.

options.text: Yes — since only one tenant runs on that specific host, it satisfies private cloud's exclusivity requirement in the only place that requirement can be measured, namely the machine the workload actually runs on.
options.why: Exclusivity applies to the surrounding cloud infrastructure NIST is describing, not to one physical machine carved out of an otherwise open platform.

options.text: Yes, because public cloud infrastructure can never contain single-tenant hardware by definition — the host must belong to some other model.
options.why: Nothing in NIST's public cloud definition forbids single-tenant hardware within it; the host being dedicated does not remove the surrounding platform from being provisioned for open use.

options.text: Yes, because it satisfies hybrid cloud instead, mixing a dedicated host with shared infrastructure inside one provider's estate.
options.why: Hybrid requires two or more distinct, bound-together cloud infrastructures with portability between them; one dedicated host inside one platform is not that composition.

items.rationale: NIST does not address single-tenant hardware inside a public platform directly, so the guide treats it as an application of the definition: the surrounding infrastructure is still provisioned for open use by the general public, which makes the dedicated host a public-cloud feature rather than a private cloud of its own, even though only one customer's workload runs on that specific machine.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 attaches both definitions to 'the cloud infrastructure' rather than to a machine: private cloud is infrastructure 'provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization', public cloud is infrastructure 'provisioned for open use by the general public'. The surrounding platform here is the latter, so the key's reading holds and o3 is false — nothing in the public-cloud definition forbids single-tenant hardware. The key and its why are honest that this is an application of the definition rather than a quotation. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A company keeps regulated data in its own self-service, metered private cloud and bursts overflow batch processing into a public provider, joined by a private network link, shared identity and a common deployment pipeline so workloads can move between the two. Does this qualify as hybrid cloud under NIST, and what would be missing if the connective tissue were removed?

options.text: Yes. Both parts are themselves clouds and are bound together by technology enabling data and application portability, which is exactly NIST's two-part test; without the connective tissue, it would be two separate estates rather than one hybrid cloud.
options.why: NIST's definition requires both conditions together: each component being a cloud, and the components being bound together for portability — and this scenario states both explicitly.

options.text: No — using more than one deployment model at once is what defines multi-cloud, not hybrid cloud, and hybrid is reserved for two providers of the same kind.
options.why: This inverts the two terms: multi-cloud varies the vendor, usually within one deployment model; hybrid varies the deployment model and, unlike multi-cloud, requires the parts to be bound together.

options.text: Yes, and the network link and shared identity are incidental details — placing workloads in two different clouds is sufficient on its own, whatever technology joins them, since NIST's composition clause is descriptive rather than a test of its own.
options.why: Placement alone is not sufficient; NIST's binding condition is a separate requirement, and removing the connective tissue would leave two separate estates rather than a hybrid cloud.

options.text: No — hybrid cloud requires a public cloud and a community cloud specifically, not a private and a public cloud, which NIST classes as something else.
options.why: NIST's composition may combine any of private, community or public; a private-plus-public pairing, as described here, is a valid and common hybrid arrangement.

items.rationale: NIST's hybrid cloud definition has two conditions that must both hold: the components must each be a distinct cloud infrastructure, and they must remain bound together by technology enabling data and application portability between them, with cloud bursting given as the worked example. This scenario states both explicitly, and removing the network link, identity plane and deployment pipeline would strip out exactly the binding condition, leaving two separate estates rather than a hybrid cloud.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 hybrid cloud: 'a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community, or public) that remain unique entities, but are bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability (e.g., cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds)'. Both halves of the key's two-part test, and cloud bursting as the worked example, are verbatim; the parenthesis refutes o4. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A retailer runs production on a public provider and keeps a completely separate analytics environment on a second public provider, with no network link, no shared identity and no data movement between them. Is this hybrid cloud?

options.text: No — this is multi-cloud only, since no private or community cloud is involved and nothing binds the two providers together.
options.why: Hybrid requires a mix of deployment models bound together; two independent public providers with no connective tissue satisfies neither condition.

options.text: Yes — using two different cloud providers for two different workloads is exactly what hybrid cloud means in everyday industry usage.
options.why: That is the loose industry usage the guide warns against; the exam-safe reading is NIST's stricter one, which this arrangement fails on both conditions.

options.text: Yes, because multi-cloud arrangements automatically qualify as hybrid once a second provider is added.
options.why: Adding a second public provider is the definition of multi-cloud, not a route into hybrid; hybrid needs a mix of deployment models and a binding condition that multi-cloud does not supply.

options.text: No, because neither environment is a private cloud, and hybrid requires at least one private cloud specifically.
options.why: NIST's composition allows private, community or public in any mix of two or more; the actual missing ingredient here is the binding condition, not the absence of a private cloud in particular.

items.rationale: Two public providers running unrelated workloads with no link, shared identity or data portability between them satisfy the definition of multi-cloud and nothing about hybrid: no private or community cloud is involved, and there is no binding technology joining the parts. The industry often calls arrangements like this hybrid loosely, but NIST's stricter reading is what the exam expects.

verification.reasoning: Two unlinked public providers fail both halves of SP 800-145's hybrid definition: there is no mix of deployment models and no binding technology 'that enables data and application portability'. AWS's multicloud page supplies the positive term — 'The use of at least two CSPs at once to operate IT solutions or workloads qualifies a customer as multicloud' — and o4's why is right that NIST's parenthesis allows any mix of private, community or public. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: An engineer proposes calling an architecture 'hybrid cloud' because it uses both a self-hosted Kubernetes cluster — with no self-service provisioning, no metering and manual capacity planning — and a public cloud provider, connected by a VPN. Is the label accurate?

options.text: No. The self-hosted cluster is not itself a cloud, since it lacks the essential characteristics such as self-service and metering, so there is only one cloud infrastructure in this picture, not the two or more NIST's composition requires.
options.why: Hybrid cloud presupposes each component already qualifies as a cloud on its own; a manually planned, unmetered cluster fails that threshold regardless of the VPN link.

options.text: Yes — connecting any on-premises infrastructure to a public cloud by VPN is what makes an architecture hybrid, whatever the on-premises side is capable of, and the VPN supplies the standardised technology the definition asks for.
options.why: A VPN link supplies connectivity, not the essential characteristics; the on-premises side must itself be a cloud before the composition can be hybrid.

options.text: Yes, and this is better described as multi-cloud specifically, since two distinct platforms are involved and each is administered separately.
options.why: Multi-cloud describes using more than one public provider; a self-hosted, non-cloud cluster paired with one public provider is neither hybrid nor multi-cloud as NIST or the industry uses either term.

options.text: Yes, because Kubernetes provides the portability layer NIST's binding condition requires — and that condition is the only one the definition imposes.
options.why: Portability tooling can help satisfy the binding condition once both sides are already clouds, but it does nothing to fix the on-premises side's failure to meet the essential characteristics in the first place.

items.rationale: Hybrid cloud requires two or more distinct cloud infrastructures, and 'cloud infrastructure' still means something meeting the essential characteristics — self-service, elasticity, metering. A self-hosted cluster with manual capacity planning and no metering is not itself a cloud, so pairing it with a public provider over a VPN produces one cloud and one non-cloud datacentre, not a hybrid composition.

verification.reasoning: SP 800-145 requires 'two or more distinct cloud infrastructures', and footnote 2 defines a cloud infrastructure as 'the collection of hardware and software that enables the five essential characteristics of cloud computing' — a cluster with manual capacity planning and no metering does not enable them, so there is only one cloud here. That footnote is the exact text refuting o2 and o4. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A team runs the same stateless web service on two public providers, but only one of the two deployments is actually tested and kept current; the other has drifted and would take days to bring back into service. A stakeholder claims 'we're multi-cloud, so we're protected against a provider outage.' Evaluate the claim.

options.text: The claim is wrong: multi-cloud does not automatically deliver high availability; a deployment that is not actually tested and ready to take over fails just as hard as a single-provider setup when its own provider goes down.
options.why: The guide states this directly: running on two providers only survives an outage if the workload is actually deployed, tested and able to fail over on both.

options.text: The claim is right — using two providers for the same workload is itself sufficient for availability across provider outages, whatever state either deployment is in on the day the outage arrives.
options.why: This treats multi-cloud as an unqualified guarantee, which is exactly the assumption the guide warns against; an untested, drifted deployment provides no real protection.

options.text: The claim is right, but only because the two deployments together form a hybrid cloud, which guarantees failover between its parts.
options.why: Two public providers with no private or community component is multi-cloud, not hybrid, and neither term guarantees failover without a tested, current standby.

options.text: The claim is wrong, but only because service level agreements do not cover multi-provider failover scenarios, which is the real gap here.
options.why: An SLA is the wrong frame entirely here — the actual gap is an untested, drifted standby deployment, not a contractual coverage question.

items.rationale: Multi-cloud reduces dependence on a single vendor in principle, but it delivers no availability benefit on its own. A workload partitioned or duplicated across providers only survives a provider outage if it is deployed, tested and genuinely able to fail over on both — an untested, drifted second deployment offers no more protection than having no second provider at all.

verification.reasoning: AWS's multicloud page defines multicloud purely as the use of at least two CSPs and lists 'Application complexity' among the challenges — 'teams must ensure that new and existing applications perform reliably across all cloud environments ... maintaining availability ... becomes more difficult' — so multicloud is nowhere claimed to deliver availability by itself, which is the key. o3 is refuted by SP 800-145, under which two public providers are no composition of distinct deployment models. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: An architecture team splits workloads across two public providers by running each application on a common container substrate with an orchestrator, so any workload could in principle run on either provider. What cost does this portability buy against, and what does it typically give up?

options.text: It spreads risk across providers, but tends to force a lowest-common-denominator architecture that gives up each provider's differentiated managed services.
options.why: The guide names exactly this trade-off: portable workloads on a common substrate spread risk but sacrifice provider-specific managed capabilities in the process.

options.text: It eliminates vendor lock-in entirely, since containers are portable by construction and carry their dependencies with them.
options.why: Portability reduces the technical component of lock-in but does not touch data gravity, egress cost or a team's accumulated platform expertise, so it does not eliminate lock-in.

options.text: It converts the architecture into a hybrid cloud, since workloads can move between the two platforms on demand.
options.why: Movement between two public providers, without a private or community component, is multi-cloud portability, not hybrid cloud, which NIST reserves for a mix of deployment models.

options.text: It removes the need for duplicated identity and monitoring tooling across the two providers, since the orchestrator supplies both.
options.why: Portability at the workload layer does not remove the operational duplication of identity, networking and monitoring that every additional provider brings with it.

items.rationale: In practice, multi-cloud workloads are either partitioned — simple, but each workload stays dependent on its own provider — or made portable on a common substrate such as containers with an orchestrator, which spreads risk but tends to force a lowest-common-denominator design, giving up the differentiated managed services either provider might otherwise offer.

verification.reasoning: AWS's multicloud page supports both halves of the key in substance: it recommends containerisation and standardised orchestration as the way to run 'the same familiar technology across multiple public clouds', and lists Interoperability ('APIs, configurations, and authentication methods vary from one provider to another') and Management complexity ('each vendor offers different tools, dashboards, APIs, and workflows') as the price — which also makes o4 false, since the page names centralised monitoring and security as separate work per provider. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: Which deployment model does NIST SP 800-145 list among its four, and which term is conspicuously absent from that list despite being common industry vocabulary?

options.text: Hybrid cloud is one of NIST's four deployment models (private, community, public, hybrid); multi-cloud is absent from that list entirely.
options.why: NIST's four named deployment models are exactly private, community, public and hybrid — the word multi-cloud appears nowhere in SP 800-145.

options.text: Multi-cloud is one of NIST's four deployment models; hybrid cloud is the industry term absent from the list.
options.why: This reverses the two: hybrid cloud is the NIST-defined model with a binding condition, while multi-cloud is the industry term NIST never defines.

options.text: Managed services is one of NIST's four deployment models; public cloud is the absent term.
options.why: Managed services is not a deployment model at all, and public cloud is very much one of NIST's four, named explicitly.

options.text: Community cloud is absent from NIST's list, while private cloud and multi-cloud are both named.
options.why: Community cloud is in fact one of NIST's four; multi-cloud is the term that is absent, not community cloud.

items.rationale: NIST SP 800-145 names exactly four deployment models — private, community, public and hybrid — and multi-cloud is not among them. That absence is itself examinable: multi-cloud is a real and useful industry term, defined directly by vendors such as AWS, but it is a consumption pattern layered on top of NIST's models rather than a fifth model of its own.

verification.reasoning: All seven pages of SP 800-145 were read: the Deployment Models section names exactly private cloud, community cloud, public cloud and hybrid cloud, and the string 'multi-cloud' (in any spelling) appears nowhere in the document. Every distractor is refuted by that list, and AWS's page supplies the vendor definition the rationale attributes to it. Refuted on first pass for the appended-`why` defect; texts rewritten.

items.stem: A platform needs to isolate ten workloads, one of which requires a Windows kernel while the other nine are fine on Linux, all on shared physical hardware. Why does this requirement rule out containers for at least one workload, and what technology does it point to instead?

options.text: A container shares the host kernel, so it cannot supply a different operating system family than the host — the Windows workload needs virtualization, giving it its own kernel.
options.why: The guide's separating axis for containers versus virtualization is exactly the kernel: containers borrow the host's, so a foreign OS family requires a technology that gives each workload its own kernel instead.

options.text: Containers rule this out because they cannot run on shared physical hardware at all, so each of the ten workloads would need a dedicated physical server of its own.
options.why: Containers run on shared hardware routinely — that is their whole appeal for density; the actual limitation is that they share the host's kernel and so cannot run a different OS family.

options.text: This points to a cloud-computing solution rather than a virtualization one — only cloud platforms can mix operating system families on shared hardware.
options.why: Mixing operating system families on one host is a virtualization capability specifically, available on-premises with a hypervisor and not dependent on being a cloud service at all.

options.text: This points to a hypervisor product recommendation, specifically a type 2 hypervisor for the Windows workload, because only a hosted hypervisor can give a guest a kernel that differs from the host's.
options.why: The requirement calls for virtualization as a technique; whether the resulting hypervisor is type 1 or type 2 is a separate, unstated question this scenario does not address, and both types give each guest its own kernel.

items.rationale: Virtualization gives each guest its own kernel, which is exactly what lets a workload run a different operating system family from its neighbours and from the host. A container, by contrast, shares the host kernel and therefore must match its family — so a Windows workload on a Linux estate needs virtualization specifically, not a denser packaging technology that cannot supply a different kernel at all.

verification.reasoning: CNCF's virtualization entry defines virtualization as taking one physical computer and running multiple isolated operating systems on it, and CNCF's container entry states containers share the same operating system, which is the key's separating axis; Red Hat's hypervisor page confirms virtualization runs on-premises with no cloud involved, refuting o3. Refuted on three counts and fixed: (1) each distractor's `why` had been appended into its own option text, so o2 and o4 refuted themselves in front of the reader; (2) o4's `why` did not address its own claim about hosted hypervisors; (3) the cited `cncf-glossary-virtualization` does not mention containers or kernels, so `cncf-glossary-container` was added as the source that actually carries the shared-kernel fact. The rewritten item was then re-checked against the same fetched sources, option by option: the key holds, no distractor is defensible, and every distractor `why` states a true fact — this verdict is recorded for the rewritten item.

items.stem: What is the precise relationship between virtualization and the hypervisor?

options.text: Virtualization is the technique of partitioning one machine into many; the hypervisor is the software layer that actually performs that partitioning.
options.why: This is the exact distinction the guide draws: one names a capability, the other names the specific program implementing it.

options.text: They are two names for the same thing — naming a product such as ESXi or KVM and naming virtualization amount to the same claim about one layer of the stack.
options.why: The guide treats conflating the two as a trap: naming a product like ESXi or KVM names a hypervisor, while the capability those products provide is virtualization.

options.text: The hypervisor is a type of container runtime specialised for running full operating systems, which is why ESXi and Docker are classified as the same category of software.
options.why: A hypervisor and a container runtime are different technologies entirely — one creates virtual machines with their own kernels, the other starts processes sharing the host kernel.

options.text: Virtualization is a cloud-only capability, whereas a hypervisor can also run outside the cloud on a single desktop or server.
options.why: Virtualization long predates cloud computing and runs on a single desktop or server with no cloud involved at all; the guide is explicit that virtualization is not itself cloud computing.

items.rationale: Virtualization is the capability — partitioning one physical machine so it can run multiple isolated operating systems. The hypervisor is the specific software layer, sitting between hardware and guests, that implements that capability, schedules real resources behind the illusion of dedicated hardware, and comes in the type 1 and type 2 varieties that classify hypervisors, not the concept of virtualization itself.

items.stem: A team wants to put a transactional database's live data files directly on object storage to save on cost per gigabyte. Why does this fail mechanically rather than merely run slowly?

options.text: Because object storage requires a filesystem to be formatted onto it before use, unlike block storage, and no filesystem can be formatted onto a key-addressed store.
options.why: This reverses the two: block storage is what a guest OS formats with a filesystem; object storage has no filesystem to format at all, addressing items by key in a flat namespace instead.

items.stem: Two application servers need to read and write the same set of files concurrently, with ordinary file permissions and locking. A second block storage volume is proposed for the second server. Why is that the wrong shape?

options.text: Object storage should be used instead, since it scales to any number of concurrent readers and writers and presents them with a mountable POSIX filesystem on which ordinary file permissions and byte-range locking work unchanged.

items.stem: A team adopts containers, an orchestrator and standard SQL specifically to reduce lock-in before choosing a cloud provider. Does this eliminate their exposure to vendor lock-in?

options.text: No — these portability layers reduce the technical component of lock-in, but they do not touch data gravity, egress cost, or the operational expertise the team will still build up around whichever provider it chooses.
options.why: The guide states this directly: portable layers reduce technical portability barriers but leave the other sources of lock-in untouched.

options.text: Yes — using only portable, standard technologies removes vendor lock-in entirely, regardless of provider, since anything expressed in standard SQL and a container image can be lifted to another platform at no cost at all.
options.why: This overstates what portability buys; even with fully portable code, the data itself and the team's accumulated platform-specific knowledge still create real costs of leaving.

options.text: Yes, because containers and standard SQL guarantee the application can be moved back to on-premises hardware at no cost, the stored data following the code automatically.
options.why: Moving back to on-premises would still involve the same data-volume, egress and re-tooling costs the guide describes; portability lowers the technical barrier, not the cost to zero.

items.rationale: Portable layers — containers, an orchestrator, standard SQL, open protocols, declarative infrastructure — reduce the technical component of lock-in by keeping the application itself movable. They do nothing, however, about data gravity, the egress cost of actually moving stored data, or the operational expertise a team accumulates around whichever platform it operates day to day, so choosing portable technology narrows lock-in without eliminating it.
